To grin is to smile very widely, usually showing your teeth. It is not a small, polite, or gentle smile — it is a big, open, full smile. When someone grins, the corners of their mouth stretch back and upward, their cheeks lift, and their teeth become visible. It is the kind of smile that takes over your whole face.
How grinning is different from smiling

Smiling is a broad word. A smile can be tiny, polite, sad, forced, or barely noticeable. You can smile with your mouth completely closed. Smiling covers a wide range.

Grinning is more specific. It is always wide and usually big. It almost always shows teeth. And while you can easily force a polite smile, a grin feels more spontaneous and genuine — it tends to break out on your face before you even decide to do it.

Think of it this way: all grins are smiles, but not all smiles are grins.
What feelings can a grin express?

This is where grinning gets interesting. A grin is not tied to just one emotion. The same physical expression — that wide, toothy smile — can mean different things depending on the situation:

Joy and happiness. This is the most common use. When a child opens a birthday gift they love, they grin. When you see an old friend after years apart, you grin. It is the natural face of pure happiness.

She walked into the surprise party and immediately began to grin.

Amusement. When something is funny — not funny enough to make you laugh out loud, but funny enough to light up your face — you grin. It is quiet, contained pleasure.

He read the joke and grinned to himself.

Mischief and playfulness. A grin can signal that someone is up to something — a prank, a secret plan, a naughty idea. This kind of grin has a slightly sly quality to it. The person knows something you do not, and they find that amusing.

The boy hid the cookie behind his back and grinned at his mother.

Satisfaction and smugness. When something goes exactly the way you wanted, especially if others doubted you, you might grin in self-satisfaction. This can feel warm if the person is likable, or slightly unpleasant if the person is being smug.

She got the highest score in the class and grinned all the way home.

Embarrassment and sheepishness. Sometimes people grin when they are caught doing something silly, or when they feel awkward. This "sheepish grin" is a mix of embarrassment and good humor — the person is laughing at themselves a little.

He tripped on the step, stood up, and grinned sheepishly at the people watching.

Nervousness. In uncomfortable or uncertain situations, some people grin as a way of coping — it is not a happy smile, but an anxious one that says, "I don't know what else to do with my face."

As a verb, grin does not take an object. You do not grin something. You simply grin, or you grin at someone or something.

  • She grinned. (basic use)
  • He grinned at her. (directed at a person)
  • They grinned at the news. (in response to something)
  • She couldn't stop grinning. (it was uncontrollable)
  • He grinned from ear to ear. (an extremely wide, joyful grin — see below)

You will also see adverbs placed right after "grinned" to tell you what kind of grin it was:

  • grinned broadly / widely — a very big grin
  • grinned sheepishly — an embarrassed, awkward grin
  • grinned mischievously — a playful, slightly sneaky grin
  • grinned wickedly — a grin with dark or bad intentions
  • grinned shyly — a grin held back a little out of shyness

This means to smile as widely as humanly possible — a grin so big it seems to stretch all the way across your face to your ears. It always signals extreme happiness or joy.

When she heard she'd got the job, she grinned from ear to ear.

This phrase means to endure something painful, unpleasant, or difficult without complaining — to put on a brave face and push through it. The "grin" here is not one of happiness; it is one of forced acceptance.

The injection hurt, but he grined and bore it without making a sound.
(Note: the past tense of grin is grinned — the 'n' is doubled.)
One small but important note on spelling

When you add -ed or -ing to grin, the final 'n' is doubled:

  • grin → grinned (past tense)
  • grin → grinning (present participle)

She was grinning all morning.
He grinned when he saw the results.

To grin is to smile widely — a big, open, often toothy smile that tends to erupt on your face naturally, without much control. It is the face of happiness, amusement, mischief, satisfaction, or even embarrassment. It is always wider and more expressive than an ordinary smile. When you see someone grinning, you know something genuine is happening on their face — some strong feeling is showing through, whether that is joy, playfulness, pride, or awkwardness.
